hints: Start by counting sugar units - think about what the endings -ose tell you and whether each sugar is built from one unit or more than one joined together.
Now think about what joins two sugar units together and how that changes the formula and number of rings - compare $C_6H_{12}O_6$ with $C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$.
walkthrough:
Sort Out One Unit Versus Two Units**
Fructose on its own is a single sugar unit, so we call it a monosaccharide. Sucrose is made by joining two monosaccharides together, glucose and fructose, so it is a disaccharide. That is the biggest structural idea.

Link Structure To Bonds, Rings And Formula**
Because sucrose is two units joined, it has two rings linked by a glycosidic bond formed by condensation, while fructose has only one ring and no glycosidic bond. That also explains the formulae: fructose $C_6H_{12}O_6$ versus sucrose $C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$.

Final answer: Fructose is a monosaccharide with one ring / $C_6H_{12}O_6$ and no glycosidic bond; sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose + fructose with two rings joined by a glycosidic bond / $C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$.

hints: Think about where T. thermophilus lives - hot springs - and what that tells you about the stability of its proteins at high temperature.
Recall what higher temperature does to molecules before denaturation happens - think kinetic energy, movement and encounters between enzyme and substrate.
Link those two ideas to factory production - why would faster encounters plus staying folded give more syrup for less cost.
walkthrough:
Why A Hot Spring Enzyme Likes Heat**
Proteins from organisms living near $95^\circ C$ have strong internal bonds so their active site keeps its precise shape at high temperature. A normal $37^\circ C$ enzyme would unfold and denature, losing its active site, but this one stays stable.

Why Heat Speeds Up Production**
Raising temperature gives all molecules more kinetic energy. Enzyme and glucose substrate move faster, so they collide more often and form more enzyme-substrate complexes per second. That means a higher rate of isomerisation to fructose and more product in the same time.

Why That Is An Advantage In A Factory**
You get two linked benefits: faster conversion and an enzyme that does not denature and can be used for longer. That lowers replacement costs and increases yield.

Final answer: Can operate at higher temperature giving more kinetic energy / more collisions between enzyme and substrate / more ES complexes, so higher rate and more product; enzyme is thermostable / less prone to denaturation so lasts longer.

hints: First find the peak of each curve - read across from 100% activity down to the pH axis for the dotted free enzyme and the solid immobilised enzyme.
Next compare the left side and right side of the peaks - at which pH values is the dotted line above the solid line, and where does it cross over.
Pick numbers to prove each difference - quote pH with % activity for both enzymes, e.g. at pH 6.0, 6.5, 8.0 and 9.0.
walkthrough:
Read The Optima**
The dotted free enzyme peaks at pH 7.5 with 100% activity. The solid immobilised enzyme peaks later at pH 8.5 with 100% activity. So immobilisation has shifted the optimum to a more alkaline pH.

Compare Below And Above The Crossover**
Up to the crossover at pH 8.0 where both are about 95%, the free enzyme is always higher. For example at pH 6.0 free is about 56% while immobilised is about 35%, and at pH 7.0 free is about 97% while immobilised is about 64%. After pH 8.0 the pattern reverses and immobilised is higher, for example at pH 8.5 immobilised is 100% while free is about 78%, and at pH 9.0 immobilised is about 96% while free has fallen to about 43%.

Describe Only, Do Not Explain**
This is a describe task, so stay with what you see: optima, which line is higher in which pH range, with paired figures and units. No need to explain why immobilisation changes charge or shape.

Final answer: Free enzyme optimum pH 7.5 and immobilised optimum pH 8.5; free has higher % activity from pH 6.0 to pH 8.0, e.g. at pH 6.5 free ~76% vs immobilised ~50%; immobilised has higher % activity from pH 8.0 to 9.0, e.g. at pH 9.0 immobilised ~96% vs free ~43%.

hints: Count the possibilities - how many different 3-base codons exist compared with how many amino acids need coding.
Think about what that maths forces to be true - can one amino acid have only one codon, or must some share several codons.
Use Table 3.2 to find a concrete alternative for the same amino acids in Table 3.1, for example another codon for tyr, glu, pro or lys.
walkthrough:
Remember The Code Is Degenerate**
There are $4^3 = 64$ possible mRNA codons but only 20 amino acids, plus 3 stop codons. That means most amino acids must be specified by more than one codon. We call this a degenerate or redundant code.

Apply It To These Five Amino Acids**
Only met with AUG as the start codon is fixed here. The others have choices: tyr can be UAU or UAC, glu can be GAA or GAG, pro can be CCU, CCC, CCA or CCG, lys can be AAA or AAG. The student just picked one possible set.

Explain The Mismatch**
The real bacterial gene could easily use a different synonymous codon for the same amino acid sequence and still make exactly the same protein. So working back from protein to mRNA does not give a unique sequence.

Final answer: Genetic code is degenerate / redundant with 64 codons for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids are coded by more than one codon; e.g. tyr UAU or UAC, glu GAA or GAG, pro CCU/CCA/CCC/CCG, lys AAA or AAG, so bacterial mRNA may use different synonymous codons.
